cases.case_name: Rippy ex rel. Rippy v. Hattaway
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: In a suit against Tennessee DCS officials, the Sixth Circuit reversed the denial of qualified immunity, holding that the plaintiffs had not identified a particularized, clearly established right that the challenged custody procedures violated.
cases.quote: a plaintiff overcomes a qualified immunity defense only by identifying a particularized, clearly established right that is violated by the promulgation and enforcement of specified procedures

relevance.FAIL-02: Sets the particularity a Tennessee plaintiff must show to overcome qualified immunity in a DCS custody case.

cases.case_name: Eidson v. Tennessee Department of Children's Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed dismissal of a father's section 1983 claims against Tennessee DCS as time-barred, holding the claims accrued at the initial removal, that continued custody was not a continuing violation, and that Heck does not delay accrual in the pre-conviction setting.
cases.quote: the rule of Heck does not apply in the pre-conviction setting to delay accrual of plaintiffs due process cause of action

relevance.INP-12: Recognizes that even a temporary custodial deprivation triggers due-process timing obligations that start the clock.
relevance.DEC-04: Identifies the removal itself as the injury that fixes the parent's cause of action.
relevance.FAIL-02: Supplies the one-year Tennessee limitations rule and accrual date that control wrongful-removal suits in this circuit.

cases.case_name: Pittman v. Cuyahoga County Department of Children & Family Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit reversed the denial of immunity, holding a social worker absolutely immune for the custody complaint, supporting affidavits and recommendations she filed with the juvenile court, even against allegations that she made intentional misrepresentations.
cases.quote: Whether Hurry made intentional misrepresentations to the juvenile court in the complaint and affidavits does not affect the conclusion that she is entitled to absolute immunity.

relevance.DEC-05: Defines the immunity that attaches to the agency's act of filing the petition and supporting affidavits.
relevance.FAIL-01: Shows that reversal of an agency's court filings rarely translates into damages liability for the worker.
relevance.FAIL-04: Limits the damages remedy against caseworkers whose court submissions preceded a bad outcome.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: In a Tennessee case, the Sixth Circuit held that social workers are bound by the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement when entering a home to investigate, that the plaintiffs alleged a violation, but that the social workers were entitled to qualified immunity because the right was not clearly established in 2008; the deputy's denial of immunity was affirmed.
cases.quote: we agree that a social worker, like other state officers, is governed by the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement

relevance.INP-03: Addresses a joint law-enforcement and CPS response to a referral at a Tennessee home.
relevance.INP-06: Shows a priority-two hotline referral that did not supply exigency for warrantless entry.
relevance.INP-12: Holds that taking protective action inside a home requires a warrant, consent, or exigency.
relevance.DEC-02: Governs how an accepted investigation may lawfully be conducted at the family's home.
relevance.DEC-04: Requires consent, exigency, or another exception before entry preceding an emergency removal.
relevance.FAIL-02: Is the controlling Sixth Circuit authority that a warrantless CPS home entry violates the Fourth Amendment.

cases.case_name: Kovacic v. Cuyahoga County Department of Children & Family Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed denial of absolute and qualified immunity to social workers who removed children without a warrant, holding it was clearly established by 2002 that the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement and its exigency exception apply to child removals.
cases.quote: it was clearly established that Fourth Amendment warrant requirements, including the exigent-circumstances exception, apply to the removal of children from their homes by social workers

relevance.INP-03: Confirms that caseworkers accompanying or acting on police information remain subject to warrant rules.
relevance.INP-12: States the clearly established rule limiting warrantless protective custody to genuine exigency.
relevance.DEC-04: Is the leading circuit authority on what exigency must exist before an emergency removal without court order.
relevance.ACT-03: Defines the constitutional predicate for lawfully placing a removed child into foster care.
relevance.FAIL-02: Holds that caseworkers lose immunity for warrantless removals absent exigent circumstances.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit reversed the denial of qualified immunity, holding that no clearly established law told caseworkers that declining to return children after a parent's implied revocation of consent to a temporary safety-plan placement violated the Fourth or Fourteenth Amendments.
cases.quote: We find that no clearly established law put the state defendants on notice that they were violating the Bambachs' Fourteenth and Fourth Amendment rights.

relevance.INP-05: Addresses a family's own temporary placement arrangement and what happens when the parent withdraws consent.
relevance.DEC-02: Shows the qualified-immunity consequences of investigative decisions made under a consent-based plan.
relevance.DEC-06: Marks the legal uncertainty surrounding non-court safety plans used in place of a petition.
relevance.ACT-01: Shows that revocation of consent to a voluntary placement does not yet carry clearly established remedies in this circuit.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that due process does not automatically require appointed counsel for indigent parents in every termination proceeding; the question is decided case by case by the trial court, subject to appellate review.
cases.quote: leave the decision whether due process calls for the appointment of counsel for indigent parents in termination proceedings to be answered in the first instance by the trial court

relevance.DEC-05: Establishes the federal floor for counsel once the State files to sever the parent-child relationship, a floor Tennessee exceeds by statute.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that a preponderance standard violates due process in parental termination proceedings and that the State must support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: We hold that such a standard adequately conveys to the factfinder the level of subjective certainty about his factual conclusions necessary to satisfy due process.

relevance.OUT-02: Is the federal constitutional source of the clear-and-convincing burden Tennessee applies in every termination case.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed a custody change based on the racial composition of the mother's new household, holding that the Equal Protection Clause forbids courts from giving effect to private racial biases in child custody decisions.
cases.quote: Private biases may be outside the reach of the law, but the law cannot, directly or indirectly, give them effect.

relevance.INP-11: Bars race-based reasoning in placement decisions except where a specific statute such as ICWA applies.
relevance.FAIL-05: Is the controlling authority prohibiting race-based placement and custody decisions.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a State to protect a child from private violence, so county social workers were not liable for failing to remove a child they knew was being abused.
cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

relevance.DEC-01: Establishes that a screen-out or closed investigation generally creates no federal constitutional liability.
relevance.ACT-03: Marks the custody line that distinguishes a child left at home from a child taken into state care.
relevance.OUT-04: Frames the State's obligations to youth as tied to custody rather than to a general protective duty.
relevance.OUT-06: Is the controlling federal authority on liability when a child dies after agency contact.
relevance.FAIL-04: Sets the constitutional limit on section 1983 claims arising from a child's death under agency supervision.
relevance.PMC-04: Explains why fatality prevention depends on statutory review commissions rather than constitutional tort remedies.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's reasonable-efforts provision does not create a right enforceable by beneficiaries through section 1983 or an implied right of action.
cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

relevance.INP-09: Explains why federal child-welfare compliance is policed through federal review rather than private suit.
relevance.INP-11: Shows that federal funding conditions are enforced administratively rather than by beneficiaries.
relevance.OUT-04: Means that federal extended-foster-care and transition obligations are generally not privately enforceable by youth.
relevance.FAIL-03: Is the controlling authority that Title IV-E noncompliance is remedied by federal administrative action, not private litigation.
relevance.PMC-01: Explains why CFSR and program-improvement plans, not lawsuits, are the primary compliance lever.
relevance.PMC-02: Frames federal audit and funding penalties as the enforcement mechanism for misuse of IV-E funds.
relevance.PMC-03: Underscores why citizen review panels matter where private enforcement is unavailable.
relevance.PMC-06: Grounds the case for external monitoring where beneficiaries have no private cause of action.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that a State may not condition an indigent parent's appeal from a decree terminating parental rights on her ability to pay record-preparation fees.
cases.quote: Mississippi may not withhold from M. L. B. "a 'record of sufficient completeness' to permit proper [appellate] consideration of [her] claims."

relevance.OUT-05: Guarantees appellate access when a parent seeks review of an adverse termination judgment.
relevance.FAIL-01: Removes a cost barrier that would otherwise prevent correction of erroneous termination orders on appeal.

cases.holding: The court held that article I, section 8 of the Tennessee Constitution protects parents' privacy in child-rearing decisions and that the State may not intervene in an intact family absent a showing of harm to the child.
cases.quote: Absent some harm to the child, we find that the state lacks a sufficiently compelling justification for interfering with this fundamental right.

relevance.INP-01: Supplies the state constitutional baseline that a report alone does not justify intrusion absent indicia of harm.
relevance.INP-02: Confirms that third-party reports cannot by themselves license state interference with a fit family.
relevance.INP-05: Protects a family that seeks voluntary help from having that contact converted into coercive intervention absent harm.
relevance.INP-12: Requires harm to the child before the State may assume protective custody under Tennessee's own constitution.
relevance.DEC-06: Supports resolving cases through non-coercive services where no harm to the child is shown.
relevance.ACT-01: Anchors the voluntariness of services in the parents' state constitutional privacy right.
relevance.ACT-05: Requires a harm finding before a court restricts a parent's contact with the child.
relevance.ACT-06: Frames state override of parental medical decision-making as permissible only on a showing of harm.

cases.holding: The court held that a natural parent generally may not invoke superior parental rights to modify a valid custody order in favor of a non-parent and must instead show a material change of circumstances making a change of custody in the child's best interests.
cases.quote: absent extraordinary circumstances discussed below, a natural parent cannot generally invoke the doctrine of superior parental rights to modify a valid order of custody

relevance.ACT-04: Explains the legal durability of a kinship or non-parent custody order once validly entered.
relevance.OUT-03: Sets the standard a parent must meet to undo a guardianship or non-parent permanency arrangement.

cases.holding: The court reversed termination, holding that both a statutory ground and best interest must be shown by clear and convincing evidence and that permanency-plan requirements supporting a substantial-noncompliance ground must be reasonable and related to the conditions necessitating foster care.
cases.quote: To terminate parental rights, a court must determine that clear and convincing evidence proves not only that statutory grounds exist but also that termination is in the child's best interest.

relevance.ACT-02: Limits court-ordered permanency-plan responsibilities to terms that are reasonable and related to the conditions that caused removal.
relevance.INP-04: Confirms that judicially imposed plan obligations are reviewable for reasonableness before they can carry consequences.
relevance.DEC-05: Frames what the agency must ultimately be able to prove when it opens and pursues a dependency-to-termination case.
relevance.OUT-01: Preserves reunification where plan noncompliance is not proven by clear and convincing evidence.
relevance.OUT-05: Supplies the evidentiary threshold whose failure requires dismissal of a termination petition.

cases.case_name: Memphis Publishing Co. v. Cherokee Children & Family Services, Inc.
cases.holding: The court held that a private nonprofit operating as the functional equivalent of a government agency in administering state child-care programs is subject to the Tennessee Public Records Act as to all of its records.
cases.quote: Cherokee's status as the functional equivalent of a governmental agency is sufficient to place it within the scope of the Tennessee Public Records Act

relevance.INP-09: Makes contractor records reachable by auditors and oversight bodies examining child-welfare spending.
relevance.FAIL-03: Provides the mechanism for exposing a contractor's noncompliance with state and federally funded program requirements.
relevance.FAIL-06: Directly addresses an agency's or contractor's refusal to disclose records.
relevance.PMC-01: Supports public access to the underlying data used in federal performance monitoring.
relevance.PMC-02: Enables audit-style review of privatized child-welfare funds.
relevance.PMC-03: Gives citizen reviewers a legal route to the records of privatized child-welfare functions.
relevance.PMC-04: Supports access to records held by private providers implicated in fatality reviews.
relevance.PMC-05: Is the leading Tennessee authority for public access to records held by private child-welfare contractors.
relevance.PMC-06: Establishes the lawful basis for obtaining the contractor records that cross-jurisdiction analysis depends on.

cases.case_name: Gonzalez v. State Department of Children's Services
cases.holding: The court held that a grandparent's motion to intervene in a juvenile court termination proceeding is governed by Tenn. R. Civ. P. 24 and affirmed the denial of intervention on that standard.
cases.quote: standing to intervene in a termination proceeding in juvenile court should be analyzed under Rule 24 of the Rules of Civil Procedure

relevance.INP-04: Fixes the procedural rule governing who may be joined when a juvenile court case is opened.
relevance.ACT-04: Determines whether relatives seeking kinship placement can become parties to the case.
relevance.DEC-05: Identifies the standard courts apply to third-party participation once a petition is filed.
relevance.OUT-03: Governs a relative's ability to participate in the proceeding that will set permanency.

cases.holding: In a wrongful-death action arising from a fatal child abuse case, the court held that the reporting statute's immunity under Tenn. Code Ann. sec. 37-1-410(a) protects only persons who actually make a report of harm, and that the physician who did not report was not immune.
cases.quote: immunity under Tennessee Code Annotated section 37-1-410(a) is afforded only to those who actually report harm

relevance.INP-01: Defines the scope and limits of Tennessee's statutory immunity for mandatory reporters.
relevance.INP-02: Confirms that reporter immunity attaches to the act of reporting, not to silence.
relevance.INP-05: Clarifies that professionals who receive disclosures but do not report gain no statutory protection.
relevance.INP-06: Shows that the immunity that encourages hotline reporting is conditioned on actually reporting.
relevance.INP-07: Applies the reporting duty and its immunity directly to a physician's evaluation of a child.
relevance.INP-08: Extends the same actually-report condition to any mandated reporter, including school staff.
relevance.INP-10: Shows the legal consequences when suspected harm is not escalated into the reporting system.
relevance.DEC-01: Illustrates the liability exposure created when suspected abuse is not reported or is screened out.
relevance.OUT-06: Arises from a child fatality and defines civil exposure for failure to report.
relevance.FAIL-04: Supplies Tennessee's rule on immunity in litigation following a child's death after an unreported disclosure.
relevance.PMC-04: Identifies failure-to-report as a recurring causal finding in child fatality cases.

cases.holding: The court reversed termination and ordered the child returned to her parents, holding that there was no willful abandonment and that only substantial harm threatening the child's welfare - not bonding with non-parent custodians during litigation - can deprive fit parents of custody.
cases.quote: only a showing of substantial harm that threatens the child's welfare may deprive the parents of the care and custody of A.M.H.

relevance.DEC-04: Sets the substantive threshold - substantial harm - that must exist before the State or a court displaces parental custody.
relevance.ACT-04: Establishes that a relative or non-parent caregiver's bond with the child does not override the parents' superior custodial rights.
relevance.OUT-01: Requires return of the child to fit parents absent proof of substantial harm.
relevance.OUT-03: Limits when a non-parent placement may harden into permanency over a parent's objection.
relevance.FAIL-05: Rejects reliance on the parents' national origin and general country conditions as evidence of harm.

cases.holding: The court held the warrantless entry lawful, setting out Tennessee's exigent-circumstances test: whether the circumstances gave rise to an objectively reasonable belief of a compelling need to act with insufficient time to obtain a warrant.
cases.quote: the inquiry is whether the circumstances give rise to an objectively reasonable belief that there was a compelling need to act and insufficient time to obtain a warrant

relevance.INP-03: Supplies the standard officers apply when entering a home during the call that generates a CPS referral.
relevance.INP-12: States the Tennessee exigency test that governs warrantless entry to take a child into protective custody.
relevance.DEC-04: Defines the objective exigency showing required to justify acting before obtaining judicial authorization.
relevance.ACT-05: Identifies when immediate action is permitted instead of seeking a court order first.
relevance.ACT-06: Includes rendering emergency aid among the recognized exigencies justifying warrantless entry.
relevance.FAIL-02: Provides the state-law benchmark against which a warrantless entry preceding removal is measured.

cases.holding: The court affirmed a finding of abandonment by willful failure to visit, holding that a parent need not be aware of the legal consequences of failing to visit for that failure to be willful, and remanded for a best-interest determination.
cases.quote: We decline to hold that a parent must be aware of the consequences of his failure to visit for such a failure to be willful.

relevance.OUT-02: Defines the willfulness element of abandonment, the most common Tennessee termination ground.

cases.holding: The court reversed termination, holding that the petitioners failed to prove by clear and convincing evidence that terminating the mother's parental rights was in the children's best interests.
cases.quote: We conclude that Father and Stepmother failed to prove by clear and convincing evidence that termination of Mother's parental rights is in the best interests of the children.

relevance.OUT-05: Shows a termination petition failing and the case ending without severance of the parental relationship.
relevance.FAIL-01: Is an appellate reversal of a termination for insufficient best-interest proof.

cases.case_name: In re Adoption of Angela E.
cases.holding: The court held that a prior order suspending the father's visitation did not prevent a finding that his failure to visit was willful, sustained abandonment by willful failure to visit, rejected abandonment by failure to support, and remanded for a best-interest determination.
cases.quote: We agree with the Court of Appeals that the prior order suspending Father's visitation rights did not preclude a finding that Father willfully failed to visit the children.

relevance.ACT-05: Shows that a protective or no-contact order restricting a parent's access does not by itself excuse the parent's failure to pursue contact.
relevance.OUT-05: Shows an appellate court sustaining one abandonment ground while rejecting another, leaving best interest undecided on remand.

cases.holding: The Tennessee Supreme Court held that the Department need not prove reasonable efforts to reunify as a precondition to termination; the extent of its efforts is instead weighed in the best-interests analysis.
cases.quote: the extent of DCS's efforts to reunify the family is weighed in the court's best-interest analysis, but proof of reasonable efforts is not a precondition to termination

relevance.ACT-02: Sets how court-ordered service and reunification efforts are legally accounted for once a plan is imposed.
relevance.ACT-03: Explains that DCS reunification efforts after a foster-care removal are evaluated in the best-interest analysis rather than as an independent element.
relevance.OUT-01: Defines the legal weight of reunification efforts when the State moves from reunification to termination.
relevance.OUT-02: Controls the elements the State must prove in a Tennessee termination case.
relevance.FAIL-03: Shows that Tennessee treats the federal reasonable-efforts requirement as a funding/oversight condition rather than a parent-enforceable element of termination.
relevance.PMC-01: Illustrates that federal reasonable-efforts expectations are enforced through funding and review mechanisms, not through the termination burden of proof.

cases.holding: The court held that due process entitles parents to fundamentally fair procedures in termination proceedings, that Tennessee's statutory right to appointed counsel plus mandatory appellate review of every ground and the best-interest finding supply that fairness, and that no collateral ineffective-assistance attack is available.
cases.quote: We hold that parents are constitutionally entitled to fundamentally fair procedures in parental termination proceedings.

relevance.OUT-02: Sets the procedural due-process framework and appellate review duty for every Tennessee termination case.
relevance.FAIL-01: Requires appellate courts to review all grounds and the best-interest finding even if unchallenged, which is how erroneous terminations are corrected.
relevance.PMC-06: Establishes that appellate review, not collateral attack, is the accountability channel for defective terminations.

cases.case_name: The Tennessean v. Metropolitan Government of Nashville & Davidson County
cases.holding: The court held that records of an open criminal investigation fall within the Public Records Act's state-law exception through Tenn. R. Crim. P. 16 and need not be disclosed while the prosecution and collateral challenges remain pending.
cases.quote: Metro is not required to disclose the requested investigative records because the records come within the Public Records Act state law exception

relevance.INP-09: Marks the limit on oversight access to records while a parallel criminal investigation is open.
relevance.FAIL-06: Distinguishes a lawful withholding from an unlawful transparency failure.
relevance.PMC-02: Identifies the exemption most often invoked against audit requests touching criminal files.
relevance.PMC-03: Tells citizen review panels which investigative records remain closed during pending prosecutions.
relevance.PMC-05: States the controlling Tennessee rule on statutory exceptions to public-records disclosure.
relevance.PMC-06: Defines the boundary any automated records-gathering must respect for open investigations.

cases.holding: The court reinstated the trial court's refusal to terminate, holding that the statutory best-interest factors are weighed according to the facts of each case and that the combined proof did not clearly and convincingly show termination was in the children's best interests.
cases.quote: the facts and circumstances of each unique case dictate how weighty and relevant each statutory factor is in the context of the case

relevance.OUT-01: Shows that a parent's progress can defeat termination and keep reunification available.
relevance.OUT-05: Explains when a termination petition must be dismissed for failure of the best-interest proof.

cases.holding: Resolving a split, the court held that Tenn. Code Ann. sec. 36-1-113(g)(14) imposes a conjunctive obligation to manifest both ability and willingness, so failure to manifest either satisfies the ground's first prong, and reinstated termination.
cases.quote: places a conjunctive obligation on a parent or guardian to manifest both an ability and willingness to personally assume legal and physical custody or financial responsibility for the child

relevance.OUT-01: Marks the point at which a parent's demonstrated inability or unwillingness to resume custody forecloses reunification.
relevance.OUT-02: Defines the elements of one of Tennessee's most frequently used termination grounds.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding that incarceration alone is not a ground and that the wanton-disregard test requires clear and convincing proof of pre-incarceration conduct displaying wanton disregard for the child's welfare, and that section 36-1-113(g)(3) applies only where the prior removal order rested on a judicial finding of dependency, neglect, or abuse.
cases.quote: Tenn.Code Ann. § 36-1-102(1)(A)(iv)'s second test for abandonment does not make incarceration alone a ground for the termination of parental rights.

relevance.DEC-03: Requires that a prior removal order rest on an actual judicial dependency, neglect, or abuse finding before it can support later grounds.
relevance.OUT-02: Is Tennessee's leading intermediate-appellate statement of the abandonment and wanton-disregard grounds, including for incarcerated parents.

cases.holding: The court held that a parent appealing a dependency and neglect adjudicatory order (including a severe child abuse finding) must file the notice of appeal within ten days of entry of the dispositional order, and that such a notice reaches issues from both the adjudicatory and dispositional hearings.
cases.quote: she needed to file her notice of appeal within ten (10) days of entry of the order on the dispositional hearing

relevance.INP-04: Fixes the timeline for challenging juvenile court orders that follow a court-initiated dependency case.
relevance.DEC-03: Addresses the severe child abuse determination that the court must make at the adjudicatory stage.
relevance.DEC-05: Distinguishes the adjudicatory and dispositional stages of a dependency petition and their review consequences.
relevance.OUT-04: Shows how the juvenile court's adjudicatory and dispositional orders structure the case that governs a youth's time in care.
relevance.FAIL-01: Supplies the timeliness rule that determines whether an erroneous dependency order can be reversed at all.

cases.holding: The court reached the unpreserved ICWA notice question because of the risk of collateral attack, found the ICWA notice and reasonable-efforts requirements satisfied on this record, and affirmed termination of the mother's parental rights.
cases.quote: Kianna's failure to raise the notice issue at trial should not preclude consideration of the issue on appeal in light of the potential for collateral attack in a subsequent proceeding

relevance.INP-11: Is the Tennessee appellate decision addressing ICWA notice when a child may be an Indian child, and why that issue survives non-preservation.
relevance.ACT-02: Reviews the reasonableness of the specific permanency-plan responsibilities imposed on the parent.

cases.case_name: Fitzpatrick v. Tennessee Department of Children's Services
cases.holding: Reviewing DCS's classification of foster parents as indicated perpetrators of neglect, the court held they received the fundamentally fair procedures due process requires through the file review and contested administrative hearing, affirmed the lack-of-supervision indication, and remanded on attorney's fees for the reversed environmental-neglect indication.
cases.quote: Procedural due process requires a government entity to employ fundamentally fair procedures whenever it acts to deprive a person of a right to or interest in life, liberty, or property.

relevance.INP-01: Shows how a report about a child in care is routed into the DCS investigative and classification system.
relevance.INP-02: Describes the statutory investigation and indicated/unfounded determination that follows any report.
relevance.INP-06: Illustrates the intake-to-classification path and the sixty-day determination deadline.
relevance.INP-07: Shows how professional observations feed the indicated-perpetrator determination.
relevance.INP-08: Applies the same investigation and classification framework to reports from any mandated source.
relevance.INP-10: Describes the escalation from report to Special Investigations Unit investigation and formal classification.
relevance.DEC-01: Explains the unfounded-versus-indicated determination DCS must make within sixty days.
relevance.DEC-02: States the statutory duty to investigate and classify every accepted report.
relevance.DEC-03: Is the controlling Tennessee decision on the preponderance standard and hearing rights attaching to an indicated finding and registry listing.
relevance.OUT-05: Shows an administrative judge reversing an indication that the evidence did not support.
relevance.FAIL-01: Demonstrates judicial and administrative reversal of an erroneous agency classification.
relevance.FAIL-06: Establishes the process owed before an agency record adverse to a caregiver becomes final.
relevance.PMC-05: Shows the administrative record-review rights that accompany an adverse DCS finding.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of the father's rights on abandonment grounds and affirmed the best-interest finding, while reversing the trial court's application of the putative-father grounds in Tenn. Code Ann. sec. 36-1-113(g)(9)(A)(iv)-(v).
cases.quote: we conclude that clear and convincing evidence supports the trial court's finding that termination of Father's parental rights was in the Children's best interest

relevance.ACT-03: Traces a drug-exposed-newborn dependency removal through to permanency.
relevance.ACT-04: Shows maternal grandparents functioning as the kinship caregivers who then seek permanency.
relevance.OUT-03: Illustrates kinship adoption as the permanency outcome following a relative placement.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed, holding that Illinois could not presume an unwed father unfit and take his children as dependents without any hearing on his fitness, because due process requires such a hearing before removal and equal protection forbids withholding it from one class of parents.
cases.quote: We have concluded that all Illinois parents are constitutionally entitled to a hearing on their fitness before their children are removed from their custody.

relevance.INP-12: Establishes that taking a child into state custody without any prior fitness hearing is the constitutional exception, not the norm.
relevance.DEC-04: Is the foundational federal authority that a hearing must precede removal, which is precisely what an exigency showing excuses.
relevance.FAIL-02: Supplies the due-process baseline against which a removal accomplished with no hearing and no emergency is measured.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court affirmed the Washington Supreme Court's invalidation of that State's third-party visitation statute as applied, holding that where a parent is fit the trial court must accord special weight to her own determination about visitation rather than substitute the judge's view of the children's best interests.
cases.quote: there is a presumption that fit parents act in the best interests of their children

relevance.INP-01: Supplies the federal presumption of parental fitness against which a bare report about an otherwise intact family must be weighed.
relevance.INP-05: Protects a parent who seeks help voluntarily from having her own judgment about her child displaced by the State's competing view of best interests.
relevance.ACT-01: Is the federal counterpart to Hawk, grounding the voluntariness of services in the constitutional presumption that a fit parent decides.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court reversed, holding that 'domicile' under the Indian Child Welfare Act is a uniform federal-law term, that twins born off-reservation to reservation-domiciled parents were domiciled on the reservation, and that the state court therefore lacked jurisdiction so its adoption decree must be vacated.
cases.quote: In enacting the ICWA Congress confirmed that, in child custody proceedings involving Indian children domiciled on the reservation, tribal jurisdiction was exclusive as to the States.

relevance.INP-11: Is the controlling federal authority on when ICWA removes a state court's jurisdiction over an Indian child's case altogether.
relevance.OUT-03: Voids a state-court permanency decree entered over a child within the tribe's exclusive jurisdiction, even where the parents arranged the placement.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: Sitting en banc, the Sixth Circuit reversed the grant of absolute immunity to a caseworker sued for concealing from the juvenile court that the mother wished to assert her parental rights, holding that absolute immunity reaches only functions performed as a legal advocate, while affirming judgment for the county.
cases.quote: absolute immunity extends to social workers only when they are acting in the capacity of legal advocates

relevance.DEC-05: Is the en banc functional framework that decides which acts surrounding the filing of a petition are absolutely immune and which draw only qualified immunity.
relevance.FAIL-04: Supplies the test a family must satisfy to reach a caseworker in damages for conduct outside her advocacy role.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed dismissal of the parents' section 1983 claims, holding that a child-abuse investigation standing alone, without removal or another deprivation of custody or control, does not infringe the constitutional right to familial association.
cases.quote: We conclude that the right to familial association is not implicated merely by governmental investigation into allegations of child abuse.

relevance.DEC-01: Explains why a screened-out or closed investigation ordinarily gives a family no federal constitutional claim.
relevance.DEC-02: Is the controlling circuit counterweight establishing that accepting a report and investigating it is not itself a constitutional injury.
relevance.INP-10: Marks the line between escalating a screening into an investigation, which is not actionable, and taking custody, which is.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the caseworker, holding that where parents voluntarily entered a safety plan and never used the plan's stated mechanism to revoke their consent, they were not entitled to any hearing.
cases.quote: the Smiths needed to explicitly withdraw the consent they explicitly gave, thus requiring Children's Services to either return the children or file a formal complaint against them

relevance.DEC-06: Is the controlling circuit authority that a genuinely voluntary safety plan used instead of a petition requires no hearing.
relevance.ACT-01: Defines what a parent must actually do to end a voluntary arrangement and force the agency either to return the child or go to court.
relevance.INP-05: Shows how a family's own agreement to a temporary out-of-home placement is treated when the parents later become dissatisfied.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding the caseworker absolutely immune for statements in the protective-custody petition and entitled to qualified immunity for warrantless in-school interviews of the child because no clearly established law in this circuit prohibited them in 2011.
cases.quote: Because Barber fails to show that these rights were clearly established at the time of the interviews, Miller enjoys qualified immunity.

relevance.INP-08: Is the circuit decision on warrantless CPS interviews of a child at school and on why damages were unavailable for them.
relevance.DEC-02: Shows the investigative steps a caseworker may take after accepting a report without incurring damages liability.
relevance.FAIL-04: Holds that where the juvenile court ordered the removal, the resulting deprivation is attributed to the court rather than to the caseworker.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit reversed the denial of qualified immunity on the Fourth Amendment claims because the law governing in-school interviews was not yet clearly established, but held going forward that the Fourth Amendment governs such interviews and requires at least reasonable suspicion, and affirmed the denial of immunity on the due-process claims arising from the safety plan.
cases.quote: At a minimum, a social worker must have reasonable suspicion of child abuse before conducting an in-school interview without a warrant or consent.

relevance.INP-08: Clarifies Barber and now requires reasonable suspicion before a social worker interviews a child at school without a warrant or consent.
relevance.DEC-06: Holds that a safety plan produced by coercion rather than genuine consent can violate procedural and substantive due process.
relevance.DEC-02: Sets the minimum factual predicate an accepted investigation must have before the caseworker may seize and question the child.
relevance.ACT-01: Is the counterweight to Smith v. Williams-Ash, marking the point at which a purportedly voluntary plan stops being voluntary.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of the mother's rights and the foster parents' adoption, holding that the due-process requirements of notice and proof of substantial harm had been satisfied and that a mother who knew of the abuse and failed to protect her child thereby committed severe child abuse.
cases.quote: The conclusion is that the constitutional requirements of notice and proof of substantial harm have been met, thus allowing the Court to intrude upon the mother's parental rights.

relevance.DEC-03: Holds that a parent who knows abuse is occurring and fails to protect the child is herself a perpetrator of severe child abuse for purposes of a founded finding.
relevance.ACT-04: Shows a long-term non-relative caregiver placement maturing into adoption once the substantial-harm threshold is met.
relevance.OUT-03: Is the doctrinal bridge between Hawk and Blair v. Badenhope on when a non-parent placement may become permanent over a parent's objection.

cases.holding: The court held the statutory definitions of willful failure to support unconstitutional because they created an irrebuttable presumption of abandonment regardless of intent, and ordered the child returned to her father under a gradual transition plan.
cases.quote: there must be a showing that the parent is unfit or that substantial harm to the child will result if parental rights are not terminated

relevance.OUT-02: States the constitutional predicate - parental unfitness or substantial harm - that underlies every Tennessee termination ground.
relevance.ACT-04: Refuses to apply a lesser standard merely because the child has spent a long period in a non-parent's custody, which is the recurring argument in kinship and foster placements.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination for abandonment by willful failure to visit, holding that abandonment must be willful and cannot be found where a parent's visitation efforts were thwarted, but that this father's failure was willful because the mother never denied him access.
cases.quote: the abandonment must be willful, and where a parent has been thwarted in visitation efforts, we have refused to find willful abandonment

relevance.OUT-02: Is the Tennessee Supreme Court source of the willfulness element of abandonment and of the thwarted-visitation answer to it.
relevance.ACT-05: Distinguishes a parent genuinely prevented from visiting from one who simply did not pursue contact, which is the question whenever access has been restricted.

cases.holding: The court held that Tennessee common law contains no law-enforcement investigative privilege capable of operating as a state-law exception to the Public Records Act, reinstated the requesters' attorney's fee award and the injunction requiring written responses, and remanded to determine which records belong to a pending criminal investigation.
cases.quote: We hold that the law enforcement privilege is not part of Tennessee common law and therefore does not operate as a "state law" exception to the Public Records Act.

relevance.INP-09: Confines the exceptions an agency may raise against an oversight body's records request to those the General Assembly actually enacted.
relevance.FAIL-06: Holds that an agency cannot invent a common-law privilege to withhold records, and that a prevailing requester recovers attorney's fees.
relevance.PMC-02: Places the burden on the government entity to justify nondisclosure of records sought in an audit-style request.
relevance.PMC-05: Is the Tennessee Supreme Court's framework for the scope of a Public Records Act request and the limits of the exceptions an entity may assert.

cases.holding: The court reversed and remanded for a new hearing, holding that a termination order must contain the findings of fact and conclusions of law required by Tenn. Code Ann. sec. 36-1-113(c) and (k) even where the parent consents, and that an appellate court cannot review the decision without them.
cases.quote: We may not conduct de novo review of the termination decision in the absence of such findings.

relevance.OUT-05: Requires that a termination judgment rest on stated findings, so a petition resolved without them cannot stand and the case returns to the trial court.
relevance.FAIL-01: Is the Tennessee Supreme Court authority requiring reversal and remand when a termination order omits the statutory findings, the most common route to correcting a defective order.

cases.holding: The court reversed the Court of Appeals and reinstated termination of the putative father's rights, holding that the Department's reunification efforts need only be reasonable rather than herculean, that parents bear a reciprocal duty to remedy the conditions requiring removal, and that clear and convincing evidence showed he could not presently assume custody.
cases.quote: The parents must also make reasonable efforts to rehabilitate themselves and to remedy the conditions that required the removal of the children.

relevance.ACT-02: Allocates the work of a court-ordered permanency plan between DCS and the parent once services are imposed.
relevance.ACT-03: Supplies the case-by-case factors for measuring DCS's post-removal reunification efforts for a child already in foster care.
relevance.OUT-01: Explains why reunification fails where the parent does not do his share, even though the agency's efforts were reasonable, and is the source of the ability-and-willingness analysis Neveah M. later builds on.

cases.holding: The court affirmed a mother's child-neglect conviction for failing to obtain medical treatment for her dying daughter, holding that the spiritual-treatment exemption in Tenn. Code Ann. sec. 39-15-402(c) is not unconstitutionally vague and that, being severable, its validity under the Establishment and Equal Protection Clauses need not be reached.
cases.quote: We hold that the spiritual treatment exemption is not unconstitutionally vague.

relevance.ACT-06: Is the Tennessee Supreme Court decision on the limits of the spiritual-treatment exemption where a child needs care, and the case in which DCS took the child into custody and authorized medical treatment.
relevance.INP-07: Shows an untreated medical condition observed by practitioners becoming the basis for state intervention and later prosecution.
relevance.OUT-06: Arises from a child's death and fixes the criminal exposure of a parent who withheld medical treatment.
relevance.DEC-03: Defines the conduct that constitutes child neglect under Tennessee law and the narrow religious exemption to it.

notes: Every case listed was retrieved from CourtListener during this session and its opinion text read; quotes are exact substrings of the majority opinion text (curly quotation marks and whitespace normalized to straight marks and single spaces).

The key_cases already present in the TN node files (e.g. 'In Re Markus E.', 'In Re Taron H.', 'In Re Ka'Myiah M.', the several bail-bonding company matters) are keyword-matched noise with synthetic citations. None survived retrieval and review, so none are carried forward. 'In re Markus E.' in particular could not be located in CourtListener's Tennessee Supreme Court index by any search run here and is therefore omitted rather than cited from memory.

Two Tennessee Court of Appeals decisions are cited in slip form because CourtListener's cluster carries no reporter citation: Fitzpatrick v. Tennessee Department of Children's Services, No. M2013-00823-COA-R3-CV (Tenn. Ct. App. Mar. 18, 2014), and In re Kentavious M., No. W2010-00483-COA-R3-PT (Tenn. Ct. App. Dec. 14, 2010). Both were used because no published Tennessee opinion on point was found - Fitzpatrick is the only retrieved Tennessee decision squarely addressing the due-process procedures attached to a DCS 'indicated' finding and abuse-registry listing, and Kentavious M. is the only retrieved Tennessee appellate decision addressing ICWA. In re Neveah M. is a published Tennessee Supreme Court opinion but CourtListener's cluster carries no S.W.3d citation, so it too is given in slip form (No. M2019-00313-SC-R11-PT).

ICWA coverage for Tennessee is thin. Only In re Kentavious M. was found, and it addresses notice (and why that issue survives non-preservation), not active efforts, qualified expert witnesses, placement preferences, or transfer to tribal court. No Tennessee decision on those elements was located; those must be argued from 25 U.S.C. sec. 1912 and 25 C.F.R. Part 23 directly. Tennessee has no state ICWA analogue identified in the node files.

Extended foster care / jurisdiction past 18 (OUT-04) has no on-point Tennessee case law found. The node is populated with the federal standard (Suter v. Artist M., foreclosing private enforcement of Title IV-E obligations; DeShaney, tying state duties to custody) plus In re Hannah S. for the juvenile-court order structure. Treat OUT-04 as governed by Tenn. Code Ann. sec. 37-2-601 et seq. and DCS policy rather than by case law.

Differential response / alternative response (DEC-06) likewise has no Tennessee case on point. It is covered by Sixth Circuit safety-plan authority - Schulkers v. Kammer (a coerced safety plan can violate due process) and Bambach v. Moegle (no clearly established remedy yet when a parent revokes consent) - which is the law a Tennessee family would actually face in federal court.

No published Tennessee decision was found on confidentiality of DCS case records under Tenn. Code Ann. sec. 37-1-409 or sec. 37-5-107, or on missing children from foster care. Records/transparency nodes are therefore built on Memphis Publishing Co. v. Cherokee Children & Family Services (private child-welfare contractors are subject to the Public Records Act) and The Tennessean v. Metropolitan Government (the state-law exception for open criminal investigative files). Both are Tennessee Supreme Court and directly usable for records requests.

Section 1983 wrongful-removal law for Tennessee sits in the Sixth Circuit and is favorable on the substantive rule but hostile on immunity. Kovacic (2013) holds the warrant requirement and its exigency exception were clearly established for child removals by 2002; Andrews v. Hickman County (2012, a Tennessee case) holds social workers are bound by the warrant requirement yet granted them qualified immunity because the point was not clearly established in 2008. Read them together and note the tension. Eidson v. Tennessee DCS fixes the one-year Tennessee limitations period running from the removal itself - the single most common bar to these claims.

Pittman v. Cuyahoga County is included because it states the Sixth Circuit rule that a caseworker's petition, affidavits and recommendations to the juvenile court carry absolute immunity even against allegations of intentional misrepresentation. Families should understand that reversal of an agency decision (FAIL-01) rarely yields damages.

Santosky v. Kramer and Lassiter v. Department of Social Services are dated here from the 'Decided' line in the opinion text (March 24, 1982 and June 1, 1981); CourtListener's cluster date_filed values for those two clusters (1982-02-22 and 1981-08-28) do not match the opinions and should not be relied on.

In re Carrington H. (Tenn. 2016) controls appellate practice: Tennessee appellate courts must review every ground and the best-interest finding even if the parent does not challenge them, and there is no collateral ineffective-assistance remedy after direct appeal. In re Kaliyah S. (Tenn. 2015) expressly abrogated prior Tennessee decisions requiring DCS to prove reasonable efforts as a precondition to termination; older Tennessee authority to the contrary is no longer good law.

FAIL-05 (discrimination/retaliation) rests only on Palmore v. Sidoti and on In re Adoption of A.M.H. (rejecting general conditions in the parents' home country as evidence of substantial harm). No Tennessee case was found on disability, religion, or retaliation in child-welfare placements; the Multiethnic Placement Act and section 504 would have to be argued without state precedent.

PMC-01 through PMC-06 are oversight/advocacy nodes with no directly governing case law. They are populated with the authorities that control the two available levers: public-records access (Memphis Publishing; The Tennessean; and now Schneider v. City of Jackson) and the non-enforceability of federal child-welfare funding conditions by private parties (Suter v. Artist M.). CAPTA citizen review panels and the Protect Our Kids Act commission have generated no litigation found here.

INP-10 (agency escalation from screening to investigation) now carries three cases - Fitzpatrick, Draper and Kottmyer v. Maas - because no further Tennessee authority on screening/escalation criteria was located.
CourtListener URLs are given in the canonical /opinion/<cluster_id>/<slug>/ form; CourtListener resolves by cluster id and redirects if a slug drifts.

Added In re Bernard T., 319 S.W.3d 586 (Tenn. 2010) for ACT-02, ACT-03, OUT-01: it is the Tennessee Supreme Court's statement that DCS reunification efforts must be reasonable rather than herculean, that parents bear a reciprocal duty to remedy the conditions causing removal, and it is the source of the manifest-ability-and-willingness analysis that In re Neveah M. later builds on. Correction to the verifier's description: Bernard T. is NOT an abandonment-by-willful-failure-to-visit case; the opinion turns on Tenn. Code Ann. sec. 36-1-113(g)(2)-(3) and the putative-father grounds in sec. 36-1-113(g)(9)(A)(iv), (vi). The willful-failure-to-visit source the verifier was reaching for is In re F.R.R. III, added separately below.

Added In re Angela E., 303 S.W.3d 240 (Tenn. 2010) for OUT-05 and FAIL-01: it holds that a termination order must contain the findings of fact and conclusions of law required by Tenn. Code Ann. sec. 36-1-113(c) and (k) even where the parent consents, and that an appellate court may not review a termination de novo without them. It is the first appeal in the same litigation as the previously cited 402 S.W.3d 636 (2013).

Added Nash-Putnam v. McCloud, 921 S.W.2d 170 (Tenn. 1996) for DEC-03, ACT-04 and OUT-03: it applies the due-process notice and substantial-harm requirements in a parent-versus-non-parent contest and holds that a mother who knew of abuse and failed to protect her child thereby committed severe child abuse.

Added In re Swanson, 2 S.W.3d 180 (Tenn. 1999) for OUT-02 and ACT-04: it states the constitutional predicate for termination (parental unfitness or substantial harm), strikes down the irrebuttable-presumption definitions of willful failure to support, and expressly refuses to apply a lesser standard merely because a child has been with a non-parent for a long period.

Added Schneider v. City of Jackson, 226 S.W.3d 332 (Tenn. 2007) for INP-09, FAIL-06, PMC-02 and PMC-05: it is the missing third leg of the records nodes, holding that no common-law law-enforcement privilege exists in Tennessee, that only statutory exceptions can defeat a Public Records Act request, and that a prevailing requester recovers attorney's fees.

Added In re F.R.R. III, 193 S.W.3d 528 (Tenn. 2006) for OUT-02 and ACT-05: it is the Tennessee Supreme Court source of the willfulness element of abandonment and of the rule that a parent thwarted in visitation efforts has not willfully abandoned the child.

Added Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000) for INP-01, INP-05 and ACT-01: it supplies the federal presumption that fit parents act in their children's best interests, the counterpart a Tennessee practitioner pairs with Hawk v. Hawk. CAVEAT: the lead Troxel opinion by Justice O'Connor is a four-Justice plurality, not a majority; the quoted presumption is the passage universally cited as controlling, but it should be cited as a plurality statement.

Added Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U.S. 645 (1972) for INP-12, DEC-04 and FAIL-02: it is the foundational federal holding that a parent is constitutionally entitled to a hearing on fitness before his children are removed, the baseline that exigency doctrine excuses and that a no-hearing removal violates.

Added Kottmyer v. Maas, 436 F.3d 684 (6th Cir. 2006) for DEC-01, DEC-02 and INP-10: it is the controlling circuit counterweight holding that a child-abuse investigation standing alone does not implicate the right to familial association, which keeps the investigation nodes from reading more favorably to families than circuit law supports.

Added Holloway v. Brush, 220 F.3d 767 (6th Cir. 2000) (en banc) for DEC-05 and FAIL-04: it is the en banc functional framework separating absolute from qualified immunity for caseworkers, on which Pittman and Barber are both decided, and the case a practitioner must cite directly rather than through Pittman.

Added Smith v. Williams-Ash, 520 F.3d 596 (6th Cir. 2008) for DEC-06, ACT-01 and INP-05: it is the voluntariness defense missing from the safety-plan nodes, holding that parents who never used the plan's stated revocation mechanism were entitled to no hearing. Read it against Schulkers (coercion) and Bambach (revocation).

Added Barber v. Miller, 809 F.3d 840 (6th Cir. 2015) for INP-08, DEC-02 and FAIL-04: it is the in-school-interview decision that Schulkers expressly clarifies, and it also holds that where a juvenile court ordered the removal the deprivation is attributed to the court rather than the caseworker. NOTE: CourtListener's cluster carries both the F.3d citation and the designation 2015 FED App. 0780N, the Sixth Circuit's marker for an opinion not recommended for full-text publication; cite it as 809 F.3d 840 but be aware of that designation.

Added Schulkers v. Kammer, 955 F.3d 520 (6th Cir. 2020) for INP-08, DEC-06, DEC-02 and ACT-01: the prior notes relied on Schulkers without carrying a verified entry for it. Retrieved and read this session: it holds prospectively that the Fourth Amendment governs a social worker's in-school interview and requires at least reasonable suspicion, while granting qualified immunity because Barber had left the law unsettled, and affirms denial of immunity on the due-process claims arising from a coerced safety plan.

Added Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield, 490 U.S. 30 (1989) for INP-11 and OUT-03: INP-11 previously rested on a single unpublished Tennessee opinion about ICWA notice. Holyfield is the controlling federal authority on ICWA's exclusive tribal jurisdiction over reservation-domiciled Indian children and on the uniform federal meaning of 'domicile'. Because no Tennessee decision on ICWA jurisdiction, placement preferences, active efforts or transfer was located, INP-11 is governed by the federal standard and must be argued from 25 U.S.C. sec. 1911-1912 directly.

Added State v. Crank, 468 S.W.3d 15 (Tenn. 2015) for ACT-06, INP-07, OUT-06 and DEC-03: ACT-06 (emergency medical/psychological care) and INP-07 (medical disclosure) were the thinnest Tennessee nodes. Crank is the Tennessee Supreme Court's decision on the spiritual-treatment exemption to the child abuse and neglect statute in a case where DCS took the child into custody and authorized medical treatment shortly before her death; it upholds the exemption against vagueness challenge and holds it severable.

Every named missing authority in the verifier's list was located, retrieved and read this session; none had to be dropped as unverifiable. The only correction is to the characterization of In re Bernard T., noted above. No authority in this pass is cited from memory.

node_map curation: to keep every node within the 2-to-6-case coverage band while adding the leading sources, four existing entries were moved out of a node's list (the case entries themselves are unchanged and each case remains mapped at its other nodes): In re M.L.P. (1057679) and In re Audrey S. (1509090) were removed from OUT-02, which now carries Santosky, Kaliyah S., Carrington H., Neveah M., Swanson and F.R.R. III - M.L.P.'s willfulness holding is now represented by its own source, F.R.R. III, and Audrey S. remains at DEC-03; Fitzpatrick (2669670) was removed from OUT-05, where it was the weakest fit (an administrative reversal rather than a dismissed petition), in favor of In re Angela E. (2010); and In re Hannah S. (2285550) was removed from FAIL-01, where it functions as an appeal-deadline rule rather than a reversal authority, in favor of In re Angela E. (2010). Hannah S. remains at INP-04, DEC-03, DEC-05 and OUT-04.

Case count: this brief now carries 48 distinct cases, above the 20-40 target, because the 33 previously verified entries were required to be carried forward unchanged and 15 leading authorities were added. No node exceeds six cases.

Remaining gaps after this pass, for a future round: no Tennessee authority was located on (a) disability, religion or retaliation discrimination in child-welfare placements (FAIL-05 still rests on Palmore and A.M.H. alone), (b) extended foster care or jurisdiction past age 18 (OUT-04), (c) confidentiality of DCS case records under Tenn. Code Ann. sec. 37-1-409 / 37-5-107, (d) differential/alternative response as a Tennessee doctrine, or (e) any ICWA element beyond notice. Each is governed by statute, regulation or federal case law rather than by Tennessee precedent.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Adoption of Female Child (Bond v. McKenzie), 896 S.W.2d 546 (Tenn. 1995) — verified to exist on CourtListener (tenn, 1995-03-20). This is the Tennessee Supreme Court's foundational statement that in a contest between a parent and a non-parent, a parent cannot be deprived of custody absent a due-process finding of substantial harm, and only then may a court reach best interests. Both Nash-Putnam and In re Swanson quote it as the source of the rule the brief attributes to them. It belongs at DEC-04, ACT-04 and OUT-03 and its absence means the brief cites the derivative cases without the root.

Missing (for a later pass): In re D.A.H., 142 S.W.3d 267 (Tenn. 2004) — verified to exist on CourtListener (tenn, 2004-08-27). It is the Tennessee Supreme Court case In re F.R.R., III cites for the thwarted-visitation rule the brief relies on at OUT-02 and ACT-05. A practitioner arguing that a parent's failure to visit was not willful cites D.A.H. directly.

Missing (for a later pass): In re D.L.B., 118 S.W.3d 360 (Tenn. 2003) — verified to exist on CourtListener (tenn, 2003-10-20). It is cited by both In re F.R.R., III and In re Angela E. as controlling on abandonment by willful failure to visit and on the limits of appellate review of a termination, and it is the standard predicate for OUT-02 and OUT-05.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Giorgianna H., 205 S.W.3d 508 (Tenn. Ct. App. 2006) — verified to exist on CourtListener (tennctapp, 2006-03-21). It is the source of the 'reasonable, not herculean' formulation that In re Bernard T. quotes and that the brief attributes to Bernard T., and it is the leading intermediate-appellate treatment of DCS reasonable efforts. It belongs at ACT-02 and ACT-03, with the caveat that In re Kaliyah S. abrogated the line of authority treating reasonable efforts as a precondition to termination.

Missing (for a later pass): Griffin v. City of Knoxville, 821 S.W.2d 921 (Tenn. 1991) — verified to exist on CourtListener (tenn, 1991-12-02). It is the Tennessee Supreme Court's leading statement that the Public Records Act contains no judicially created privacy balancing test and that exceptions must come from the General Assembly. It is the doctrinal predecessor to Schneider and belongs at FAIL-06, PMC-05 and INP-09, which currently rest on Schneider alone for that proposition.

Missing (for a later pass): Doe v. Sundquist, 2 S.W.3d 919 (Tenn. 1999) — verified to exist on CourtListener (tenn, 1999-09-27). It is the Tennessee Supreme Court's decision on the state constitutional privacy interest in sealed adoption records, and it is the closest Tennessee authority to the confidentiality gap the brief identifies at PMC-05 and FAIL-06 (no case found on Tenn. Code Ann. sec. 37-1-409 or sec. 37-5-107). It should at minimum be evaluated for those nodes.
